newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran could see first woman minister in new cabinet.
newsitem.headline: Iran could see first woman minister in new cabinet.

text.p: Iran's incoming president Mohammad Khatami said on Tuesday he had begun consultations on forming his cabinet and indicated the Islamic republic might get its first woman minister.

Khatami, a moderate Shi'ite Moslem clergyman elected on a tide of hopes for change after 18 years of Islamic revolution, said he would later present his list of ministers to Iran's supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei and then the cabinet would be introduced to parliament for final approval.
"Our country is a vast country and there are great tasks ahead," he said at his first news conference since his election by a landslide on Friday.
Khatami, due to succeed President Akhbar Hashemi Rafsanjani in August, said he hoped to be able to use all the experience available in the country in forming his cabinet.

Asked whether he would appoint a woman as a minister, Khatami said the government had a clear duty to provide equal opportunities to women. He had highlighted women's issues during his campaign which gained him wide support among women voters.
"I see no impediment to their presence in the highest possible positions in the country. Therefore opportunities are left with their capabilities and not their gender," he said.

Iranian analysts have speculated that if Khatami appoints a woman as a minister it could be the country's most prominent female politician, Rafsanjani's daughter Faezeh Hashemi, who was elected on her own landslide of votes in last year's parliamentary elections.
Khatami said the huge number of votes he won -- 69 percent of the 29 million turnout -- was a matter of honour and he felt a heavy burden of duty.
He said it was quite natural that he would be committed to the programme he had introduced in the election campaign.

The 12-point manifesto includes eradicating discrimination, equal opportunities for all, familiarising people with their human rights and legal freedoms, social security for the protection of the underprivileged, continuation of economic construction, the implementation of the rule of law and responsive government.
Emphasising his strong commitment to Iran's Islamic revolution, Khatami said it took place with the participation of the men and women of the country. "It was not imposed on the people," he said.
Outgoing president Rafsanjani is due to become head of a high state council which will draw up long-term policies and advise Khamenei who has absolute power over all state institutions.
This has led to speculation that Rafsanjani's might become the second highest office in the country after Khamenei and higher than the new president's.

Addressing this point, Khatami said: "The leadership (Khamanei) is on the top of the system and the president would be the second person and with the blessing of God there is unity in our system and powers of the executive, legislature and judiciary."
He added that Rafsanjani was one of the most prominent figures of the revolution and the Islamic republic and would maintain a high spiritual value wherever he was.
